sermon:
There is a moment when you hand a newborn to a man who has just become a father, and his hands do not know what to do. The weight is small. The terror is not. He is holding something infinite to him and impossibly fragile at once. John opens his Gospel by asking us to hold something far stranger than that. He asks us to hold the eternal God in a body small enough to nurse.

Most biographies begin with a birth. John begins before time. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). He reaches behind Genesis itself. Before there was a beginning, the Word already was. Not made. Not summoned. Was. And then John does the thing that should have stopped the pen in his hand.

**The God Who Could Be Touched**

John 1:14 says, "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth." Read that slowly. The Word that spoke galaxies into existence became flesh. Not a costume of flesh. Not a temporary disguise. Flesh — with all its hunger and exhaustion and tears. The verb John uses for dwelt carries the sense of pitching a tent, the way God's presence once filled the tabernacle in the wilderness. The glory that Israel could not approach on Sinai now had a face you could look at across a table.

We want a God who stays at a safe height. A God at altitude does not embarrass us. He does not get hungry in our kitchen or weep at our funerals. But the God of John 1 came down into the body, and the body is where we are most ashamed and most afraid. I am ashamed of my body when it fails. I am afraid of it when it sickens. And into that exact place, the infinite God arrived.

**The Light That Was Not Received**

John does not pretend this arrival was welcomed. "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him" (John 1:11). The Maker walked into the world He had made, and the world did not recognize its own carpenter. This is the indictment, and I am inside it. I have stood in rooms where Christ was present in a suffering person, in a convicting word, and I did not recognize Him. I wanted Him in the abstract, at a height, not in the flesh asking something of me.

But the verse does not end in rejection. "But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God" (John 1:12). The same God who was not received still gives. The reception is not earned by the deserving. It is given to the believing.

This is the whole Gospel in seed. John will spend twenty chapters showing you signs and sayings, but he has already told you the verdict in the first paragraph: the infinite God took on a body you could touch. Everything that follows — water into wine, sight to the blind, Lazarus walking out of his tomb — is commentary on that one impossible sentence.

The Christ connection here is not drawn from the text. It is the text. There is no Jesus behind the curtain of John 1. He is the Word, He is the light, He is the life, named plainly. To miss Him is to miss the only point John is making.

So here is what remains. You do not have to climb to find God. He has already descended. The light has come into your room, into your body, into the Tuesday you are dreading. The only question John leaves on the table is whether you will receive Him or, like His own, fail to see who is standing in front of you.

The Word moved into the neighborhood.

A man came to Jesus at night. John tells us that detail twice, and he means it both ways. Nicodemus came in the dark because he did not want to be seen, and he came in the dark because that is where he was living. He was a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, a teacher of Israel. He had spent his life improving himself by the Law, and he had done it well. He is the best version of the religious project. And Jesus tells him it is not enough.

Nicodemus opens with a compliment. He has Jesus filed under teacher, under sign-worker, under impressive. Jesus does not accept the category. He cuts past the flattery to the only thing that matters.

**Improvement Will Not Save You**

"Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3). Nicodemus hears it the way we all hear it first. He thinks about returning to the womb, about the impossibility of starting his biology over. He is being literal because the spiritual claim is too large. He came expecting Jesus to add something to his already impressive life. Jesus tells him he needs to start over entirely.

This is the offense, and it is aimed at the religious before anyone else. Nicodemus is not a sinner off the street. He is the man who kept the rules. And to that man Jesus says the rules will not get you in. You cannot improve your way across the line. A corpse does not need a workout plan. It needs life. A man born once into Adam's death needs a second birth into something he cannot manufacture.

I feel the sting of this as a pastor, because my whole instinct is to coach people toward a better version of themselves. Jesus refuses that ministry. He will not hand Nicodemus a self-improvement program. He tells him to be born from above, which is the one thing no person has ever done for himself. No one chose his first birth. No one engineers his second.

**Born of the Spirit**

"The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit" (John 3:8). The word for wind and the word for Spirit are the same word. Jesus is telling Nicodemus that new birth is the work of the Spirit, free and sovereign, not summoned by his effort. You feel the wind. You do not command it.

And then Jesus grounds it in something specific. He reaches back to the wilderness, to the bronze serpent Moses lifted on a pole so the dying could look and live. "So must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life" (John 3:14–15). The new birth is not a vague spirituality. It is born from the cross. You are made alive by looking at the One lifted up for you.

This is where John 3:16 lands, and we have heard it so often it has gone numb. God so loved the world that He gave His Son, so that whoever believes would not perish. The verse is not a refrigerator magnet. It is the mechanism of the new birth Nicodemus could not perform. God gives. We believe. We live.

The Christ connection is the serpent on the pole. Jesus names Himself as the thing lifted up so the dying can look and be born again. He does not point to a method. He points to His own crucifixion as the source of new life.

Nicodemus came at night and left, John tells us, still in the dark. He does not believe yet. But he shows up again in chapter 19, helping to bury Jesus, carrying spices in daylight. The wind had blown after all.

So stop trying to be a better version of a dead man. You do not need improvement. You need a new birth, and it is not yours to make.

You must be born from above.

Jesus was tired and thirsty, sitting alone by a well in the heat of the day, in a region Jewish travelers went out of their way to avoid. John tells us He had to pass through Samaria. The Greek carries a necessity, and it was not a necessity of geography. There were other roads. He had to pass through because a woman was coming to that well at noon, and noon is the wrong time to draw water.

Women came to the well in the cool of the morning, together, in conversation. She came alone in the heat. The timing tells her story before she says a word. She is avoiding the other women, and the other women are avoiding her. By the end of the chapter we learn she has had five husbands and is living with a man who is not her husband. She is the person the town has filed away.

**He Went Where He Did Not Have To Go**

A Jewish rabbi was not supposed to be alone with a Samaritan woman, and certainly not this one. Jesus crosses three barriers in a single sentence. He speaks to a Samaritan. He speaks to a woman. He speaks to a sinner the community had quietly written off. "Give me a drink" (John 4:7). He asks her for help. He puts Himself in her debt before He says anything about her need. The God who needs nothing makes Himself thirsty in front of the woman everyone avoided.

I want to feel my own avoidance here. There are people I have crossed the road to miss. People whose reputation gave me permission not to look at them. Jesus had every cultural permission to ignore this woman, and He spent it walking toward her instead. He did not come to Samaria by accident. He came because she was there.

**Living Water for the Empty Bucket**

Then He moves the conversation off the surface. "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water" (John 4:10). She has been coming to this well for years, hauling buckets, and going home thirsty again every afternoon. Jesus tells her there is a water that ends the cycle. "Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again" (John 4:14).

She has been trying to fill the same emptiness with husband after husband, and it keeps draining out. Jesus names it gently and exactly. He tells her to call her husband, and when she says she has none, He tells her the truth she has been hiding at noon for years. He does not flinch from her history, and He does not leave her in it.

Then He gives her what He gave almost no one else openly. She mentions the Messiah who is coming. "Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he'" (John 4:26). The first clear declaration of His identity in this Gospel is not spoken to a council or a crowd. It is spoken to a Samaritan woman with five failed marriages, beside a well, at noon. The Christ connection is His own self-disclosure. He is the living water. He is the Messiah, and He says so to the least likely audience in the book.

She leaves her water jar. That detail matters. She came for water and forgot the bucket, because she finally found the thing the bucket was always failing to hold. She runs to the town that shunned her and tells the very people she had been avoiding to come and see.

The woman everyone avoided became the first evangelist in Samaria. Grace ran downhill, to the bottom, to her, and from her it ran back up the hill to the whole town.

He went where He didn't have to go.

Two sisters sent the same message and got the same silence. Lazarus was sick, and they sent word to Jesus, knowing He loved their brother, knowing He could heal from a distance. And Jesus, who loved them, stayed where He was two more days. By the time He arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. In the thinking of that time, the soul lingered three days. Four days meant it was over. No hope, no loophole, no near miss. Dead and decaying.

Martha meets Him on the road with the sentence both sisters had been rehearsing. If you had been here, my brother would not have died. It is faith and grief tangled together. She believes He could have. She cannot understand why He did not.

**The God Who Weeps**

Mary comes and says the same words, and falls at His feet weeping. And here John gives us the shortest verse in the Bible, and one of the most staggering. "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). The One who knew, in the next ten minutes, He would call Lazarus out of the grave, stood at that grave and cried. He was not weeping because the situation was hopeless. He held the solution. He wept anyway.

This undoes the lie that faith means you do not grieve. Jesus knew the ending and still wept at the tomb. He was, the text says, deeply moved and troubled. The Greek suggests something like anger, a fury at death itself, at the wreckage it makes of the people He loves. God in the flesh stood in front of a grave and hated it. If you have stood at a graveside and felt your faith and your tears fighting each other, you are standing where Jesus stood. He did both at once.

I have been the pastor saying the right words at the graveside while something in me wanted to shout at the casket. I used to think that was a failure of faith. John 11 tells me it is the heart of God. He does not despise the tears. He cried them first.

**The Voice That Empties Graves**

Before the tomb, Jesus says to Martha the line that the whole chapter is built around. "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). Notice He does not say He gives resurrection, as if it were a gift He distributes. He says He is resurrection. The thing the sisters are waiting for at the last day is standing in the road talking to them. Resurrection has a face, and it is His.

Then He proves it. He has them roll away the stone, over Martha's protest about the smell, and He calls into the dark. "Lazarus, come out" (John 11:43). The dead man hears. He walks out still wrapped in his grave clothes, and Jesus tells them to unbind him. The voice that spoke light into the void in chapter one now speaks into a tomb, and death lets go.

This is the seventh and greatest sign in John, and it points straight ahead. Jesus weeps at this grave, and within days He will weep no more, because He will go into a tomb of His own. The One who calls Lazarus out will be carried in. But the same voice that emptied Lazarus's tomb will not stay silent in His own. The Christ connection is the order of events: He wept at the tomb He would open, and then He walked out of His own.

Lazarus came out still bound, and would die again someday. Jesus came out with the grave clothes folded, and death was finished. The sign was never the point. The One the sign pointed to was.

So bring your grief to the only One who hates the grave more than you do, and holds the keys to it.

He wept at the tomb He would open.

It was the last evening. Jesus knew, John tells us, that His hour had come, that the Father had given all things into His hands, that He had come from God and was going back to God. Read that list again. It is a coronation inventory. All things in His hands. Come from God. Returning to God. This is the moment a king would seize his crown. And John tells us what Jesus did with all that authority. He got up from the table, took off His outer garment, tied a towel around His waist, and knelt down to wash dirt off the feet of men who would abandon Him before morning.

Foot washing was the lowest job in the house, assigned to the lowest servant. The roads were dust and worse, and feet in open sandals carried all of it. No rabbi did this. No host did this. It was beneath everyone in the room. And the One who held all things in His hands picked up the basin no one else would touch.

**The Throne Was a Basin**

John frames it as deliberate. "Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands... rose from supper" (John 13:3–4). The kneeling is not a moment of weakness or low self-image. It flows directly out of His authority. He washes feet because He knows exactly who He is. Power, in His hands, bends down. This is the opposite of every instinct I have. When I am certain of my standing, I want to be served. When I am secure, I expand. Jesus, fully secure, contracted into a servant's posture.

Peter cannot bear it. "Lord, do you wash my feet?" and then, "You shall never wash my feet" (John 13:6, 8). Peter's refusal sounds like humility. It is actually pride. He would rather not be served by a kneeling Lord, because being served puts him in the position of the helpless. Jesus answers, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me." You do not get to keep your dignity and have Christ too. You come to Him as the one with dirty feet, or you do not come.

That is the part I resist. I will serve. I would rather serve than be washed. Being washed means admitting I came in filthy, that I cannot clean myself, that the King has to kneel for me. Peter wanted to skip that. So do I.

**Now Do the Same**

When He finished, He put His garment back on and asked them a question. "Do you understand what I have done to you?" (John 13:12). Then He gave the command. "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet" (John 13:14). He turns the basin over to them. The kneeling was not only mercy shown to them. It was a pattern handed to them. The greatness of the kingdom is measured in towels, not titles.

And John has already told us, before the washing, that the devil had put it into Judas's heart to betray Him. Which means Jesus washed the feet of His betrayer. He knelt in front of Judas, ran water over the feet that would walk out and sell Him, and dried them with a towel. He served the man already plotting His death.

The Christ connection is the cross in miniature. The towel and the basin are the same downward motion as Calvary. He who was in the form of God knelt to wash feet on Thursday and would be lifted up to wash sin on Friday. The basin was a rehearsal for the blood. Both are the same King going lower than anyone thought God would go.

So the question is not whether you admire the kneeling Christ. The question is whether you will let Him wash you, and then pick up the towel He hands you.

The throne was a basin.

Crucifixion was designed to end in a scream. Rome built it to break men slowly, to drag the dying out until the body finally gave up in exhaustion and shame. Most who died on a cross went out with a groan or a curse or nothing at all. Jesus went out with a verdict. John, who stood close enough to hear it, records the word. Not a cry of defeat. A declaration of completion.

"When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, 'It is finished,' and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit" (John 19:30). In the Greek it is one word, tetelestai. It was the word written across a bill when the debt was paid in full. Paid. Done. Nothing remaining. The dying man on the middle cross announces that a transaction has closed.

**Not a Defeat to Be Reversed**

We are tempted to read the cross as the low point that the resurrection later fixes, as if Friday were the loss and Sunday the comeback. John will not let us read it that way. For John, the cross is the hour of glory. All through this Gospel Jesus has spoken of being lifted up, and He meant the cross. The lifting up onto the wood is itself the throne. "It is finished" is not a man hoping someone will rescue him. It is a King saying the work is done.

What was finished. The debt of sin that no person could pay. The wrath that hung over the guilty. The long account that ran from Eden forward, the one I have added to with every sin I have committed and every good I have left undone. I keep trying to finish my own account, to add enough to balance it. The cross tells me the ledger is already closed, and I had nothing to put in it. Tetelestai is an offense to the self-made. It means there is nothing left for me to contribute. It is finished means stop trying to finish it.

John even notes that they did not break His legs, as they broke the legs of the men beside Him, because He was already dead. He points to the Scripture: not one of His bones would be broken. The Passover lamb was prepared with no broken bones. John is telling us plainly what is happening on that cross. The Lamb of God, announced back in chapter one, is being slain. The sign was never the point. This is the point.

**And Then He Rose**

But the verdict is not the whole sentence. On the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and found the stone removed. She thought His body had been stolen. Then He spoke her name, and grief turned over into recognition. The same voice that said it is finished now says, Mary.

Later that week Thomas, who would not believe without proof, was given the proof. "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe" (John 20:27). The wounds were still there. The risen Christ kept the marks of the finished work in His body. He did not rise as if the cross had not happened. He rose carrying it, vindicated.

This is the Christ connection, and it is the spine of the whole Gospel. John tells us exactly why he wrote all of it. "These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (John 20:31). The signs, the sayings, the cross, the empty tomb, all of it was aimed at one response in you. Believe Him, and live.

So the cross was not a wound that needed healing. It was a victory that needed announcing, and the resurrection is the announcement. The debt was paid Friday. The receipt was delivered Sunday.

Finished — and then He rose.
